extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of creative writing, narratology, and literary analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and designing how a narrative orders and paces events in time (anticipation, retroversion, achrony) and how story-time (TS) relates to fabula-time (TF) via five tempi (ellipsis, summary, scene, slow-down, pause). Useful for writers and critics concerned with pacing, suspense, and temporal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (internal vs external)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipations can be internal or external; they signal something that will occur later and may generate uncertainty that is effectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal anticipations often complement a future ellipsis or paralipsis (things are made clear now so later can be skipped) or mark "I shall be coming back to this." External anticipations point ahead in the fabula. Use anticipations to link scenes or to foreshadow; manage uncertainty to create emotional suspense (e.g., waiting phases in Duras).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is presented as the first in a series, prompting the reader to expect repetition (e.g., "a spectacle that would weigh on our spirits every Friday from now on").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a detailed 'first' that justifies its detailed presentation as exemplar of recurring events; avoid giving so much unique detail that the iterative character is undermined (too much detail makes repetition implausible). Iterativity also allows showing a scene through a newcomer's eyes to increase plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcements vs hints
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements are explicit pointers that something will happen later (use of adverbs like 'later', verbs like 'expect' or 'promise'); hints are implicit germs whose anticipatory force is only seen later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announcements work against suspense; hints increase it because trained readers will question whether a detail is anticipatory. Balance explicit announcements and implicit hints depending on desired suspense. Use announcements when you want to diminish mystery; use hints to initiate a game between story and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: False hints / red herrings
rubrics_metrics.description: Details that suggest they are clues but turn out to be irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use false hints to manipulate the reader's curiosity in detective or puzzle narratives; ensure attentive readers still have a possibility to glimpse true anticipations to keep the game fair. Example: Hawthorne's impulses that turn out irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achrony (deviations of chronology that cannot be analysed)
rubrics_metrics.description: An achrony is a deviation of time for which direction, distance, or span cannot be determined; the presentation and fabula linearities no longer correspond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achrony can result from undated statements, grouping by non-chronological criteria (e.g., spatial, associative), or complex combos of anticipation/retroversion that defy sorting. Use achrony to reflect frozen temporality (e.g., trauma) or to resist linear conceptions of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation-within-retroversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreshadowing that occurs inside a back-reference (a forward reference embedded within a retroversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can verge on achrony when it evokes an expected present that contrasts sharply with the realized present, enabling confrontation between expected and realized states and suggesting meta-narrative commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroversion-within-anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A retroactive reference embedded within a forward-looking anticipation (we are told beforehand how a present will later be interpreted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates foreshadowing that points to a future revelation; at the moment of revelation, the past is referenced in relation to the future-shaped present — useful to prepare the reader for reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation that is retroversion in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: An event that is chronologically future in the fabula has already been presented in the story (e.g., in embedded speech), making it an anticipation relative to the fabula but a retroversion relative to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complex relation can complicate directionality and contribute to achronal effects; use carefully to play with narrative levels and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undated achrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Achrony in which no indication of direction, distance, or span is given (e.g., 'I have never seen him without his wig').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaves temporal relation indeterminate; useful to create timelessness or narrative opacity but reduces analyzability of chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-chronological grouping (spatial/associative ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grouping events by spatial location or association rather than chronological order, producing achrony within an otherwise chronological narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces visual or associative narrative flows (Proust, Woolf); treat such series as achronies when chronology elsewhere is marked — can be used to foreground perception or theme rather than sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring rhythm: TF vs TS (time of fabula vs story-time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate speed of presentation by juxtaposing time covered by fabula (TF) with amount of text devoted (TS) — analogous to speed = distance/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise calculation is often pointless; use it to understand attention patterns. TF/TS comparisons reveal which episodes receive greater attention and thus narrative emphasis. Use dialogue (approximate isochrony) as a zero-line for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall rhythm analysis (distribution of attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many pages/lines are devoted to each episode to see which parts of a life-story or fabula receive more attention and how rhythm matches content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify episodes given disproportionate narrative time (e.g., childhood summarized, first love dwelt on). Rhythm should reflect thematic or psychological priorities; mismatches can produce ironic or modernist effects (Flaubert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five narrative tempi (ellipsis, summary, scene, slow-down, pause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every narrative segment corresponds to one of five tempi defined by relations of TF and TS: Ellipsis (TF >> TS, omitted), Summary (TF > TS), Scene (TF ≈ TS), Slow-down (TF < TS), Pause (TF << TS with no fabula-time movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narrative segments to analyze pacing. Use these categories to explain how attention and narrative time are manipulated; be mindful that boundaries are flexible (pseudo-ellipsis/mini-summary) and scenes often include non-synchronous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (complete omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: No indication in the story of the amount of fabula-time skipped; the reader deduces omission (e.g., 'When I was back in New York after two years...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipses may be used for painful, unutterable events, denial, or to speed narrative. They can be signaled by retroversions or explicit time markers; beware pseudo-ellipsis (mini-summary) that approaches summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (accelerated presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick enumeration of events that covers much fabula-time in little text; useful for background, connecting scenes, or pushing through less significant events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summary to prepare for a key turning point that will be presented extensively. Dramatic climaxes should be presented as scenes; routine or insignificant events can be summarized. The type of fabula (crisis vs developing) affects how much summarizing is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (scenic presentation / near-isochrony)
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed presentation in which TF and TS are roughly the same; scenes function as central narrative moments and building blocks of longer narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes often incorporate retroversions, anticipations, and non-narrative fragments; they can serve as examples of recurring events (turning into anticipations) or be used to show routine via repetition. Avoid attempting true synchronicity (unreadable); omit dead time and trivial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow-down (temporal magnification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rare tempo that stretches presentation beyond simultaneity to magnify perception (e.g., a kiss rendered in long descriptive detail); often highly evocative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly at moments of great suspense or intense perception. Slow-downs can occur within scenes (a sequence of thoughts between ring and door) and may replace the fabula with intense sensory or epistemological analysis (Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause (description/argument with no fabula-time movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative sections where the fabula does not move forward; attention focuses on an object/description or argument while story-time remains stationary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pauses retard narrative flow and were standard in Naturalist/modernist writing; they can be concealed by tying description to a perceiving actor (verb of perception) to imply time passage and avoid appearing as outright interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching rhythm to thematic/psychological content
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm should reflect or comment on the subject matter (e.g., Flaubert's reversal of expected rhythm to reflect boredom; traumatic temporality using achrony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately choose tempos and distributions of attention so that pacing underscores theme, mood, or character psychology. A reversal or mismatch between expected rhythm and presented rhythm can produce irony, modernist or postmodern effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-ellipsis / mini-summary (borderline cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that signal a skipped time (e.g., 'Two years passed.') but which may include content specification that moves them toward summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the flexible borderline between ellipsis and summary; expand or contract such passages depending on desired rhythm and level of explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as anti-linear / pseudo-scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes that function as anti-linear moments or are presented as scenes but actually contain many invisible ellipses (pseudo-scenes) — e.g., Camus's L'étranger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pseudo-scenes to create the impression of scenic immediacy while compressing fabula-time via invisible ellipses to achieve effects like emptiness or rapid time passage.
